findings.title: Endpoints whose page lists this plan and that the key could not call
findings.statement: 3 of the 21 endpoints inventoried answered HTTP 403 with `error_code` 1006 — "your API key subscription plan doesn’t support this endpoint" — although their documentation pages list the plan this key is on. Each refusal was recorded rather than inferred, and is quoted below. For a consumer this is a planning matter: an endpoint a page lists cannot be assumed callable, so the coverage of a plan is worth one verifying call before a check is built on it. This project made those calls in T1.2 and T1.3 and adapted the checks that depended on them (D2).

findings.title: E12 answered a parameter error to every call this project made to it
findings.statement: E12 (`/v1/dex/token-liquidity/query`) answered HTTP 400 with `error_code` 400 and the message "Parameter error" to every call recorded here, including one made with its documented parameters alone. This is not a plan refusal: the code is 400, not 1006. The message names no parameter, so a consumer has no way to tell which value was not accepted; naming it would make the difference between a retry and a dead end. This project does not use this endpoint (D10).

findings.title: E08 answered HTTP 400 on part of the recorded calls
findings.statement: 1 of the 3 recorded answers of E08 (33.3 %) carried HTTP 400 with `error_code` 400 and the message "Please provide either a dex id or dex slug.", over 1 distinct request(s) on 2026-09-24T16:06:40.933Z. Every one of them reported `credit_count` 0, so they were not charged. The consequence for a consumer is that a check resting on this endpoint needs an answer for the case where the call brings nothing back: this project reports the check as `unavailable` with the reason it gave, rather than scoring the asset as though the call had succeeded (D9).

findings.title: E10 answered HTTP 500 on part of the recorded calls
findings.statement: 41 of the 77 recorded answers of E10 (53.2 %) carried HTTP 500 with `error_code` 500 and the message "The system is busy, please try again later!", over 14 distinct request(s) between 2026-09-26T10:44:13.710Z and 2026-09-26T10:51:32.376Z. The client retries a call that brings nothing back, which is why the answers outnumber the requests. Every one of them reported `credit_count` 0, so they were not charged. The consequence for a consumer is that a check resting on this endpoint needs an answer for the case where the call brings nothing back: this project reports the check as `unavailable` with the reason it gave, rather than scoring the asset as though the call had succeeded (D9).

findings.title: The `status` block arrives in two shapes
findings.statement: Across the recorded answers, `status.error_code` arrives as a string on 13 endpoint(s) (E02, E03, E06, E08, E09, E10 and 7 more), with no `notice` field, and as a number on 4 endpoint(s) (E01, E05, E07, E20), with a `notice` field beside it. Both shapes carry `timestamp`, `elapsed` and `credit_count`, and both were observed on accepted calls, so the difference is in the envelope rather than in what it reports.

evidence.shows: string on E02, E03, E06, E08, E09, E10 and 7 more
number on E01, E05, E07, E20

findings.title: A client reading `status.error_code` needs to accept both a number and a string
findings.statement: A consumer that compares `status.error_code` with the number 0 succeeds on one group of endpoints and fails on the other. Reading it through a comparison that accepts both — as this project does in `src/cmc/status.ts` — costs one function and removes the difference at the edge of the client. Publishing one shape on every endpoint would remove it once for every consumer.

evidence.shows: the string shape, on E02, E03, E06, E08, E09, E10 and 7 more
the number shape, on E01, E05, E07, E20

findings.title: Every accepted answer reported the cost this project reserves for its endpoint
findings.statement: Over the 301 accepted answers of 17 endpoints, `status.credit_count` matched the per-call cost reserved for each one, with no exception. E01, E13, E20 reported 0 on every answer, which is what their pages state and what makes an identifier lookup free to a consumer. A consumer can therefore budget a run from the documented per-call cost and check it against the answers as they arrive, which is what the credit meter of this project does.

findings.title: Endpoints that took a large share of a ten-second budget when called one at a time
findings.statement: 9 endpoint(s) have an answer taking at least half of the 10 s one `check` is allowed (D1), measured on the captures recorded one call at a time, where nothing but the API is inside the interval: E14 up to 9.5 s (median 2 s over 4 answer(s)), E01 up to 9.5 s (median 4.7 s over 5 answer(s)), E20 up to 7.9 s (median 1.3 s over 5 answer(s)), E06 up to 6.5 s (median 1.4 s over 6 answer(s)), E05 up to 6.5 s (median 1.4 s over 6 answer(s)), E02 up to 6.3 s (median 485 ms over 6 answer(s)), E19 up to 6.1 s (median 362 ms over 34 answer(s)), E03 up to 5.9 s (median 5.9 s over 1 answer(s)), E10 up to 5.1 s (median 646 ms over 4 answer(s)). The consequence is a call plan rather than a complaint: this project sends the independent calls of one asset in parallel and keeps the slowest endpoints off that path (D1, D10).

measurement.label: slowest answer called one at a time

findings.title: Upper bounds observed during a run that paced its own requests
findings.statement: During the calibration capture(s), which wait for a free request slot inside the measured interval, 1 further endpoint(s) recorded an answer past half of the 10 s budget: E11 up to 10 s. These are upper bounds on what the API took and are reported as such: the wait is inside the number, so nothing here says the API was slow.

findings.title: Assets that reach `ACT` on fewer checks than the rest
findings.statement: 19 asset(s) of the sample reached `ACT` with fewer than 5 of the seven checks evaluated: BTC (3 of 7), ETH (3 of 7), XRP (3 of 7), ZEC (3 of 7), HYPE (3 of 7), DOGE (3 of 7) and 13 more. The score renormalises over the checks that ran and prints the coverage beside the verdict, so nothing is hidden; but two `ACT` verdicts are not the same reading, and the coverage line is what tells them apart. Whether thin coverage should hold a verdict back is the question D9 left open and T4.2 answered for the top fifty; this is where the case can be watched.
